claims.text: A nanoscale Cu interlayer can mediate the transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
Introducing a Cu interlayer alters interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
A Cu interlayer induces interfacial strain gradients that facilitate dislocation nucleation at high temperatures.
HEA multilayers with highly coherent interfaces normally transition gradually from diffusion-controlled creep at lower temperatures to dislocation-mediated creep at elevated temperatures.
Cu has sufficient lattice mismatch with the HEA layers to introduce localized interfacial strain.
The ductility of Cu contributes to reduced interface coherency.
The Cu interlayer disrupts diffusion pathways at the interface.
The inherent ductility of Cu promotes localized dislocation nucleation.
The Cu-induced change in interfacial structure lowers the activation barrier for dislocation-mediated creep.
Lowering the activation barrier causes dislocation-mediated creep to begin earlier than in a fully coherent HEA multilayer.
HEA multilayers containing a Cu interlayer will transition to dislocation-mediated creep at a lower temperature or lower strain than comparable multilayers without the interlayer.
The earlier transition will be accompanied by increased dislocation density and corresponding changes in creep rate.
In HEA multilayers without an interlayer, temperature and stress alone govern the gradual shift from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
The proposed effect of the Cu interlayer exists only within a specific interlayer-thickness range.
An excessively thick Cu interlayer may dominate the multilayer properties, whereas an excessively thin interlayer may not alter interface coherency effectively.
Direct experimental validation of this Cu-interlayer mechanism in HEA multilayers is currently lacking.
The selection of Cu is extrapolated from behavior in conventional alloy systems rather than demonstrated in HEA multilayers.
